title: Create an awareness of enviromental protection

lessons.title: Why the environment needs protecting
lessons.html:
Why the environment needs protecting

The environment is everything around us: soil, water, air, plants, animals and people. We depend on it for food, water, clean air and work. In horticulture we work with the environment every day, so we can damage it or help protect it.

Main environmental problems in South Africa

  • Water shortage: South Africa is a dry country. Droughts and water restrictions are common. Wasting water hurts everyone.
  • Water pollution: fertiliser, pesticides, oil and waste washing into rivers, dams and groundwater.
  • Soil erosion: bare soil washed or blown away. Topsoil takes a very long time to form.
  • Invasive alien plants: plants from other countries, such as some wattles, lantana and pompom weed, that spread and push out indigenous plants and use a lot of water.
  • Loss of indigenous plants and animals: when veld and wetlands are cleared or damaged.
  • Waste and litter: plastic, garden waste dumped in the veld, burning that pollutes the air.

The law

South Africa has laws to protect the environment. The National Water Act 36 of 1998 protects our water resources. The Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 deals with soil, veld and the control of weeds and invader plants. The Constitution gives everyone the right to an environment that is not harmful to their health. Your employer will tell you the rules that apply on your site.

Example

A landscaping team washes out a fertiliser spreader and a spray tank next to a stream. The chemicals kill fish and frogs downstream, and the water is not safe for cattle. One careless act harms many people and animals.

lessons.title: Protecting the environment at work
lessons.html:
Protecting the environment at work

Save water

  • Water early in the morning or late afternoon, when less water evaporates.
  • Fix leaks in taps, pipes and sprinklers quickly, and report them.
  • Do not water paving, roads or walls. Adjust sprinklers.
  • Use mulch on beds to keep soil moist.
  • Plant water-wise and indigenous plants where possible.

Use chemicals carefully

  • Only trained workers mix and apply fertilisers and pesticides, following the label.
  • Do not spray when it is windy or rain is coming.
  • Never wash equipment or empty tanks near rivers, dams, drains or boreholes.
  • Return or dispose of empty containers as the label and your site say. Never reuse them for water or food.

Protect soil

  • Do not leave soil bare. Plant, mulch or cover it.
  • Control water runoff on slopes.
  • Use compost to build healthy soil.

Manage waste

  • Compost garden waste instead of burning or dumping it.
  • Do not compost invasive weeds with seeds; follow your site's rules for them.
  • Sort recyclable waste: plastic pots, bottles, metal.
  • Pick up litter.
  • Put oil, fuel and chemical waste in marked containers.

Protect plants and animals

  • Learn to recognise invasive alien plants and report them.
  • Do not damage indigenous trees and wetlands.
  • Leave birds' nests, frogs, lizards and bees alone where it is safe.
  • Do not kill snakes. Call a trained person to remove them.

Spread the word

Tell co-workers, clients and your family why these things matter. Report pollution and damage to your supervisor.

Key points

  • South Africa is a dry country; save water.
  • Keep chemicals and waste out of rivers, drains and boreholes.
  • Protect soil from erosion with plants, mulch and compost.
  • Compost garden waste and sort recyclables.
  • Report invasive plants, pollution and environmental damage.
